incidents.title: Payment service timeout under load
incidents.description: During a flash sale, the payment service started returning 504 Gateway Timeout errors for roughly 15% of requests. Latency on the /charge endpoint spiked from 200ms to over 12s. Traffic was about 6x normal peak load.
incidents.root_cause: The database connection pool for the payments service was capped at 20 connections. Under load, requests queued waiting for a free connection and eventually timed out at the load balancer before ever reaching the DB.
incidents.resolution: Increased the connection pool size to 100, added a circuit breaker to fail fast when the pool is exhausted, and added pool utilization to the on-call dashboard so it's caught before it becomes customer-facing.

incidents.title: Checkout API 504s during traffic spike
incidents.description: Checkout API began throwing 504s intermittently starting around 2pm, coinciding with a marketing email blast. Error rate climbed to 20% over 10 minutes before auto-recovering when traffic dropped.
incidents.root_cause: Same pattern as the payments incident â€” checkout shares the same Postgres connection pool config, which was never bumped after the payments fix was rolled out to that service.
incidents.resolution: Applied the same connection pool increase (100 connections) and circuit breaker pattern used in the payments fix. Added a checklist item to propagate infra config fixes across all services sharing the same DB cluster.

incidents.title: Memory leak in notification worker
incidents.description: The notification worker pod's memory usage climbed steadily over 6 hours until it hit the container limit and was OOMKilled by Kubernetes. This repeated roughly every 6 hours, causing brief gaps in email delivery.
incidents.root_cause: An event listener was being re-registered on every message processed instead of once at startup, causing listener objects (and their closures) to accumulate and never get garbage collected.
incidents.resolution: Moved listener registration outside the message-processing loop so it only runs once at startup. Added a memory usage alert at 80% of container limit to catch future leaks before they cause OOMKills.

incidents.title: Report generation service OOMKilled repeatedly
incidents.description: The nightly report generation job has been getting OOMKilled twice a week for the past month, always partway through processing the largest customer accounts. Jobs auto-restart but produce incomplete reports.
incidents.root_cause: Similar failure mode to the notification worker leak â€” a caching layer intended to avoid recomputation was never evicting old entries, so memory usage grew unbounded across a single job run.
incidents.resolution: Added an LRU eviction policy with a hard cache size limit. Also added a memory alert modeled on the one added for the notification worker incident.

incidents.title: Homepage cache stampede after deploy
incidents.description: Immediately after a routine deploy, the homepage cache was flushed and response times spiked to 3-4s for about 90 seconds as thousands of concurrent requests all hit the database at once trying to regenerate the same cached page.
incidents.root_cause: Deploys clear the entire cache instead of only invalidating changed keys, and there was no lock/single-flight mechanism to prevent duplicate concurrent regeneration of the same cache entry.
incidents.resolution: Implemented request coalescing (single-flight) so only one request regenerates a given cache key while others wait for that result. Also switched to selective cache invalidation on deploy instead of a full flush.

incidents.title: Product listing page slow after deploy
incidents.description: Product listing page latency jumped from 300ms to 2.5s right after a deploy, gradually recovering over about 2 minutes as things settled.
incidents.root_cause: Same cache stampede pattern seen on the homepage â€” the product listing page shares the same deploy-time full cache flush and had no coalescing protection either.
incidents.resolution: Extended the single-flight coalescing fix from the homepage incident to cover the product listing cache keys as well.

incidents.title: Auth service outage from expired TLS certificate
incidents.description: All login attempts started failing with SSL handshake errors at 3am. The internal auth service was completely unreachable from other internal services for 40 minutes until the on-call engineer manually renewed the cert.
incidents.root_cause: The internal TLS certificate for the auth service expired. There was no automated renewal and no expiry monitoring in place for internal-only certificates.
incidents.resolution: Set up automated certificate renewal via cert-manager with a 30-day-before-expiry renewal window, and added expiry monitoring alerts for all internal certs, not just public-facing ones.

incidents.title: Internal API gateway cert expiry outage
incidents.description: Service-to-service calls through the internal API gateway began failing overnight with TLS errors, taking down several dependent services for about 25 minutes.
incidents.root_cause: Another internal-only TLS certificate expired, on the API gateway this time. This was the same monitoring gap identified in the auth service incident â€” the fix from that incident hadn't been rolled out gateway-wide yet.
incidents.resolution: Extended cert-manager auto-renewal and expiry alerting to cover the API gateway and all remaining internal services, closing the gap left after the auth incident.

incidents.title: Search results degraded from third-party rate limiting
incidents.description: Search results started falling back to a generic 'no results' state for about 30% of queries during a 2-hour window. No errors in our own logs, just empty responses from the search relevance API.
incidents.root_cause: A third-party search relevance API silently rate-limited us after we increased query volume from a new feature launch, and our client had no retry/backoff logic or rate limit monitoring for that dependency.
incidents.resolution: Added exponential backoff with retry for the search relevance API, plus alerting on 429 response rates from third-party dependencies so rate limiting is caught immediately instead of silently degrading UX.

incidents.title: Recommendation engine silently degraded
incidents.description: The recommendation widget started showing the same fallback 'popular items' list for all users. No alerts fired because the endpoint was still returning 200 OK responses.
incidents.root_cause: Same pattern as the search incident â€” a third-party ML scoring API began rate limiting us after a traffic increase, and we had no retry/backoff or rate-limit alerting for that dependency either.
incidents.resolution: Applied the same backoff and 429-rate alerting pattern used for the search relevance API fix to the recommendation engine's third-party dependency.

incidents.title: Database disk full causing write failures
incidents.description: Write operations across multiple services began failing with database errors. Read operations were still working. The primary Postgres instance had run out of disk space.
incidents.root_cause: Write-ahead log (WAL) files had accumulated far beyond expectations because a replication slot to a decommissioned read replica was never dropped, so Postgres kept retaining WAL files indefinitely for a replica that no longer existed.
incidents.resolution: Dropped the orphaned replication slot and added a monitoring check that alerts when a replication slot's lag or retained WAL size exceeds a threshold, and a quarterly audit of active replication slots.

incidents.title: Race condition causing duplicate order creation
incidents.description: A small number of customers were charged twice and had two identical orders created when double-clicking the checkout button or refreshing during submission.
incidents.root_cause: The order creation endpoint had no idempotency key or database-level uniqueness constraint, so two near-simultaneous requests both passed the initial 'does this order exist' check before either had committed.
incidents.resolution: Added a client-generated idempotency key required on order creation requests, plus a unique database constraint on (customer_id, idempotency_key) as a hard backstop against duplicate orders.

incidents.title: Resolved: Payment API started returning 504 timeouts again during
incidents.description: Payment API started returning 504 timeouts again during a flash sale; latency on the /charge endpoint spiked from 200ms to over 12s for about 15% of requests.
incidents.resolution:
1. **Likely root cause (hypothesis)**
Database connection pool exhaustion in the payments service triggered by the high traffic volume of the flash sale. Requests to the `/charge` endpoint are getting stuck queuing for an available database connection, eventually exceeding the load balancer timeout threshold (12s+) and returning 504 Gateway Timeouts to clients.

2. **Suggested fix (concrete steps)**
- **Immediate Mitigation:** Increase the maximum database connection pool size for the payments service (e.g., scale up to 100 connections) and restart/redeploy the payments service instances to apply the configuration change.
- **Fail-Fast Protection:** Ensure the circuit breaker is active for the payment connection pool to fail fast with a 530/503 error when the pool is exhausted, rather than letting requests queue until load balancer timeout (504).
- **Capacity Verification:** Check the database server's overall `max_connections` limit to confirm that increasing the payment service's connection pool won't exhaust total database limits under autoscaling.
- **Monitoring:** Inspect the payment service dashboard for connection pool wait times and pool utilization to ensure the new threshold accommodates flash sale peak concurrency.

3. **Matched past incident(s)**
- **id 6 / "Payment service timeout under load"**: Direct match for the same service (`payments`) and failure mode. Under high traffic, a restricted connection pool caused requests to queue waiting for database connections, leading to load balancer timeouts (504s) and severe latency spikes.
- **id 7 / "Checkout API 504s during traffic spike"**: Highly relevant secondary match demonstrating the exact same pattern (connection pool bottleneck causing 504 timeouts during traffic spikes) on a neighboring service sharing DB infrastructure configurations.

4. **Match Assessment**
Past incidents 6 and 7 are strong direct matches for this issue.

incidents.title: Resolved: Checkout API throwing 504s during a traffic spike
incidents.description: Checkout API throwing 504s during a traffic spike right after the flash sale where the payment service timed out — same connection pool pattern we fixed before.
incidents.resolution:
1. **Likely root cause (hypothesis)**
The Checkout API's database connection pool is under-provisioned or exhausted due to the high concurrency of the flash sale traffic spike. Requests to the Checkout API are queuing while waiting for an available Postgres connection, eventually exceeding the load balancer's timeout threshold and resulting in 504 Gateway Timeouts.

2. **Suggested fix (concrete steps)**
- **Immediate Mitigation:** Increase the maximum database connection pool size for the Checkout API service (e.g., scale up to 100 connections) and redeploy/restart the service instances to apply the configuration change.
- **Fail-Fast Protection:** Ensure a circuit breaker is active on the Checkout API connection pool so that requests fail fast when the pool is exhausted rather than queuing until upstream 504 load balancer timeouts occur.
- **Capacity Verification:** Check the central Postgres database cluster's overall `max_connections` limit to confirm that raising pool limits across Checkout and Payment services won't exceed total DB connection limits.
- **Configuration Audit:** Review all microservices sharing the Postgres cluster to confirm that connection pool size and timeout configurations are aligned across services.

3. **Matched past incident(s)**
- **id 7 / "Checkout API 504s during traffic spike"**: Direct match for the exact service (`checkout`) and error pattern. The Checkout API suffered 504 timeouts during a traffic spike because its connection pool was not updated when the payment service fix was rolled out.
- **id 22 / "Resolved: Payment API started returning 504 timeouts again during"**: Direct evidence of a recurring failure pattern (`Resolved:` prefix) where flash sale traffic spikes exhaust DB connection pools and trigger 504 timeouts across the checkout and payment pipeline.
- **id 6 / "Payment service timeout under load"**: Original foundational match detailing how a capped connection pool (20 connections) causes request queuing and load balancer timeouts under traffic spikes, establishing the 100-connection pool and circuit breaker fix.

4. **Match Assessment**
Past incidents id 7, id 22, and id 6 are clear, direct matches for this issue. No alternative diagnostic search is required.

incidents.title: Resolved: Notification worker pod memory climbing steadily again until
incidents.description: Notification worker pod memory climbing steadily again until Kubernetes OOMKills it, roughly every few hours, causing gaps in email delivery.
incidents.resolution:
1. **Likely root cause (hypothesis)**
A memory leak in the notification worker service, likely caused by event listeners, callbacks, or per-message state being re-registered or accumulated inside the message processing loop instead of being initialized once at startup. As messages are processed over time, uncollected objects accumulate in the heap, causing memory to steadily climb until Kubernetes terminates the container with an OOMKill.

2. **Suggested fix (concrete steps)**
- **Inspect event listeners/handlers:** Audit recent commits to the notification worker to verify whether event listeners, closures, or logger objects are being registered within the per-message processing loop.
- **Refactor registration logic:** Move any listener or subscription logic out of the message handler into the worker initialization/startup routine so it only runs once per pod lifecycle.
- **Capture heap dumps:** Take a heap dump from a running notification worker pod as its memory usage increases to confirm the accumulating object types.
- **Verify alerts and resource limits:** Ensure container memory limit alerts (e.g., at 80% limit) trigger early, and monitor pod restarts post-fix to confirm steady memory consumption.

3. **Matched past incident(s)**
- **id 8 / "Memory leak in notification worker"**: Direct match on service (`notifications`), service type (`notification worker`), and identical symptom profile (steady memory accumulation leading to periodic Kubernetes OOMKills). Incident 8 was caused by re-registering event listeners on every processed message, which matches the recurrence indicated in the new incident description.

4. **Relevance assessment**
N/A — Past incident **id 8** is a direct match.

incidents.title: Resolved: Nightly report generation job OOMKilled partway through processing
incidents.description: Nightly report generation job OOMKilled partway through processing the largest accounts, similar to the notification worker memory leak — the same caching issue.
incidents.resolution:
1. **Likely root cause (hypothesis)**
The report generation service is using an in-memory cache to avoid recomputation while processing account data, but the cache lacks an eviction policy (or maximum memory boundary). When processing particularly large accounts, entries accumulate unbounded throughout the job run, eventually exceeding the container memory limit and causing Kubernetes to terminate the pod with an `OOMKilled` status.

2. **Suggested fix (concrete steps)**
- **Configure cache eviction policy:** Add an LRU (Least Recently Used) eviction policy and set a strict hard upper limit on cache size or entry count within the reporting service's caching layer.
- **Explicit cache flushing:** Ensure cache entries or temporary per-account context are cleared after each account or batch processing step completes.
- **Set up memory alerts:** Implement container memory utilization alerts (e.g., triggering at 80% of limit) on the reporting worker pods to catch runaway memory growth before OOMKills occur.
- **Validate with large datasets:** Run a test execution against the largest account datasets while monitoring heap/memory usage to confirm memory stabilizes under load.

3. **Matched past incident(s)**
- **id 9 / "Report generation service OOMKilled repeatedly"**: Direct match on service (`reporting`), symptom (OOMKilled during large job runs), and root cause (caching layer intended to avoid recomputation failing to evict old entries, leading to unbounded memory growth).
- **id 24 / "Resolved: Notification worker pod memory climbing steadily again until"** and **id 8 / "Memory leak in notification worker"**: Secondary match referenced in the prompt and incident notes regarding the underlying pattern of unbounded memory accumulation in background workers, though id 9 is the exact match for the reporting service caching failure.

4. **Relevance assessment**
Past incident **id 9** is a direct match and provides the exact resolution required.
